lesson_title: Reading the Stats Sheet: Analysing Partnership Statements
hook_text: The shop made R421 000. Good year or lazy year? The stats sheet knows.
clip_script: A netball coach never watches every match a player ever played. She reads the stats sheet — goals per game, passes completed. Small numbers standing for a big performance. That is what analysis does to a business. Profitability is goals per game: out of every hundred rand of sales, thirty-three survive paying for the goods, and about seventeen reach the owners. Then the tempo section: one rand does a lap — becomes stock, waits 42 days on the shelf, becomes a customer's promise, waits 13 days more, comes home as cash. Meanwhile the supplier gets paid at day 24, so from day 24 to day 55 the shop runs the lap on its own money. And the verdict questions: can it survive? Four times cover on the bills — safe, maybe too safe, with R130 000 dozing in the bank. Was it worth it? The partners' money earned 57,3 percent; the bank would have paid nine. But here is the coach's first rule, the whole subject in one line: a stat means nothing alone. Every number needs a next-to — last year, the plan, the rival. No comparison, no meaning. Comparison, cause, advice — that is how marks are scored.
visual_style: A coach's clipboard morphing into financial statements, stat tiles flipping like scoreboards, a rand coin running laps around shelf, promise and bank icons with day-counters ticking; energetic court-side palette.
pacing: Quick stat flips, a steady lap sequence with counters, then a decisive verdict beat.
